title: Adapter Pattern
tagline: Wrap an incompatible interface in a translator so existing code works with new third-party APIs without a single change to the caller.

sections.content:
**The Problem:** You have code that expects a specific interface — say, a `PaymentProcessor` with a `charge(amount, currency)` method. A new payment provider ships an SDK where the equivalent call is `makePayment({ total: amount, curr: currency })`. Rewriting every call site is risky and tedious. Changing the SDK is impossible.

**The Adapter pattern** solves this by introducing a *wrapper class* that implements the interface your code already expects, and internally translates each call to the incompatible API. Your existing code sees nothing new — it keeps calling `charge(amount, currency)` — while the adapter quietly converts and delegates. Think of it as a **language translator**: both parties speak their native tongue; the adapter bridges the gap.

This is one of the most common patterns in real production code. Every time you integrate a third-party library, a legacy module, or an external service whose API doesn't match your domain model, you are a candidate for the Adapter.

sections.caption: OrderService depends only on PaymentProcessor. StripeAdapter implements that interface and translates calls to the real Stripe SDK — OrderService never changes when you swap providers.

sections.title: The Power Socket Adapter
sections.content:
You bring a laptop from the US to Europe. The plug shape is incompatible — you cannot simply force it into the wall socket. A **travel adapter** sits between the two: your US plug goes in one side, the European socket on the other. Neither the laptop nor the wall was modified. The adapter is pure translation.

In software, your existing code is the laptop (it expects a specific interface). The third-party SDK is the European socket (it has a different API). The Adapter class is the travel adapter — it makes them fit together without altering either side.

**Participants:**

- **Target Interface** — the interface your existing client code already depends on (e.g., `PaymentProcessor` with `charge(amount, currency)`). It defines the contract the rest of the system understands.
- **Adaptee** — the incompatible class or module you want to use (e.g., a third-party `StripeSDK` with `createCharge({ amount, currency })`). You cannot or do not want to modify it.
- **Adapter** — a concrete class that implements the Target Interface and holds a reference to the Adaptee. Each Target method is implemented by translating the call and forwarding it to the Adaptee.
- **Client** — your existing code (e.g., `OrderService`) that calls the Target Interface. It never knows an Adapter exists.

**Object Adapter vs. Class Adapter:** In JavaScript (and most OO languages) you implement an *Object Adapter* — the adapter wraps the adaptee via *composition* (holds a reference). Some languages allow a *Class Adapter* via multiple inheritance, but composition is preferred because it keeps coupling loose and allows swapping the adaptee at runtime.

**Key insight:** The Adapter does not add behaviour — it only translates. If you find yourself adding significant logic inside an adapter, that logic probably belongs in a Service or Decorator instead.

sections.caption: The call flows through the adapter invisibly. OrderService speaks the target interface language; StripeSDK speaks its own language. StripeAdapter is the interpreter.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: OrderService is unchanged whether you use Stripe or PayPal. Each adapter translates the unified `charge(amount, currency, note)` interface to the specific SDK call. Adding a new provider means writing one new adapter class — no edits to OrderService or any other caller.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The skeleton shows the four participants in their pure form. The adapter holds the adaptee via composition (not inheritance of the adaptee) and the client is completely isolated from the adaptee's interface.

sections.content:
**When to use:** Integrating third-party SDKs, legacy modules, or microservices whose API shape differs from your domain model. Also essential when writing testable code — an adapter around a real HTTP client lets you swap in a fake in tests.

**When NOT to use:** If you control both sides of the interface, just align them directly — an adapter adds an indirection layer that has a small cognitive cost. Avoid creating adapters that contain significant business logic; that's a sign the work belongs in a service layer.

**In the wild:** Express middleware adapters, React's `useRef` adapting DOM APIs, `Array.from()` adapting iterables, Node.js stream adapters, and virtually every ORM that wraps a raw database driver.

items: The **Adapter** pattern converts one interface into another so incompatible classes can work together without modifying either side.
Use **composition** (object adapter) over inheritance: hold a reference to the adaptee and delegate — this keeps coupling loose and adaptees swappable at runtime.
The client only sees the **Target interface** — it is completely shielded from the adaptee's API, making provider swaps and testing trivial.
Adapters should contain **translation only**, not business logic — keep them thin wrappers.
Common real-world uses: third-party SDK integration, legacy system bridges, and test doubles that replace real external dependencies.

quiz.question: What is the primary problem the Adapter pattern solves?
options: Adding new behaviour to an object without subclassing
Allowing classes with incompatible interfaces to work together
Controlling access to an object
Simplifying a complex subsystem behind a single facade
quiz.explanation: The Adapter pattern makes two incompatible interfaces compatible by introducing a wrapper that translates calls from one interface to another.

quiz.question: In the Adapter pattern, which participant is the class your client code already depends on?
options: Adaptee
Adapter
Target Interface
Client
quiz.explanation: The Target Interface is the contract your existing client code already understands. The Adapter implements this interface while internally using the Adaptee.

quiz.question: Why is an Object Adapter (composition) preferred over a Class Adapter (multiple inheritance) in JavaScript?
options: JavaScript does not support classes
Composition keeps coupling loose and allows swapping the adaptee at runtime
Multiple inheritance always causes stack overflows
Class adapters cannot implement interfaces
quiz.explanation: Composition means the adapter holds a reference to the adaptee — that reference can be any conforming object, making it easy to swap implementations (e.g., in tests). Class adapters via inheritance lock you to a specific adaptee class.

quiz.question: You add significant discount-calculation logic inside an adapter class. What problem does this indicate?
options: The adapter is correctly combining two responsibilities
Business logic belongs in the adaptee, not the adapter
The logic should be in a service layer, not the adapter — adapters should only translate
This is a valid use of the Strategy pattern
quiz.explanation: Adapters should be thin translators only. Embedding business logic in an adapter violates Single Responsibility and makes the logic hard to find and test independently.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a real-world example of the Adapter pattern?
options: A Singleton database connection pool
An ORM that wraps raw SQL driver calls behind a model interface
A recursive algorithm that traverses a tree
A pub/sub event emitter
quiz.explanation: An ORM (like TypeORM or Sequelize) wraps the incompatible raw database driver API behind a clean domain model interface — this is the Adapter pattern in production.

quiz.question: After adding a new payment provider (PayPalAdapter), how many lines of OrderService need to change?
options: All lines that call charge()
The constructor only
Zero — OrderService depends on the Target interface, not the concrete adapter
Only the import statements
quiz.explanation: This is the core benefit: the client (OrderService) is decoupled from all concrete adapters. You inject a new adapter; the client code is untouched.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use the Adapter pattern?
options: When integrating a third-party SDK
When you control both sides of the interface and can align them directly
When writing testable code with fake implementations
When wrapping a legacy module
quiz.explanation: If you own both interfaces, simply align them. An unnecessary adapter adds an indirection layer and cognitive overhead without benefit.

quiz.question: The Adaptee in the Adapter pattern is best described as:
options: The interface the client already depends on
The wrapper class that translates calls
The incompatible class you want to reuse without modifying
The client that initiates requests
quiz.explanation: The Adaptee is the existing class with an incompatible interface — typically a third-party library or legacy module you cannot or do not want to change.

quiz.question: How does the Adapter pattern aid unit testing?
options: It eliminates the need for test doubles
It lets you inject a fake adapter instead of calling the real third-party SDK
It auto-generates mocks from the Target interface
It makes all methods public for test access
quiz.explanation: Because the client depends on the Target interface, you can inject a simple fake object in tests that implements the same interface without triggering real network or payment calls.

quiz.question: Which structural relationship defines the Object Adapter?
options: Adapter inherits from both Target and Adaptee
Adapter implements Target and composes (holds a reference to) the Adaptee
Client extends Adapter
Adaptee implements Target directly
quiz.explanation: The Object Adapter implements the Target interface (so the client can use it) and holds a reference to the Adaptee via composition (so it can delegate to the incompatible API).
